newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: FOCUS - Mauritius forecasts rise in sugar production.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mauritius forecasts rise in sugar production.

text.p: The Chamber of Agriculture in the Indian Ocean island of Mauritius on Tuesday forecast sugar production to rise to 610,000 tonnes this year compared to 590,000 tonnes in 1996 and 540,000 tonnes in 1995.
It said in a statement the total sugar cane harvest in Mauritius for calendar 1997 was estimated at 5.6 million tonnes, with an extraction rate of 10.90 percent.

The Chamber's statement came ahead of a ceremony on Wednesday to mark the start of the 1997 harvest, to be presided over by Prime Minister Naive Ramgoolam and Agriculture Minister Arvin Boolell. The two will cut the first two canes at the start of the harvest.
The sugar cane harvest usually stretches from June to December.
The Mauritius Sugar Syndicate exported 6,163 tonnes of sugar in April compared to 22,967 tonnes in March and 7,175 in April 1996, the Public Relations Office of the Sugar Industry (Prosi) reported.
Prosi said that out of total exports for April, 5,213 tonnes were consigned to European Union countries and 381 tonnes to United States. The balance went to the world market.
Mauritius earned some 8.02 billion rupees ($387 million) from sugar exports in 1996. That was a huge proportion of the total 31.99 billion rupees in export earnings in that period.
There have been no forecasts for earnings this year.
In his 1997/98 state budget this month, Mauritian Finance Minister Vasant Bunwaree proposed the removal of a levy on the sugar industry introduced last year.

Bunwaree said removal of the levy was necessary because the sugar industry, an important source of government revenue, had not registered previously expected windfall gains in 1996. Introducing the levy last year, the government had forecast the levy would raise up to 300 million rupees ($14.6 million) on windfall gains.

But Bunwaree said: "The sugar industry has made the case that there has been no windfall gains on the 1996 crop. In view of this unexpected turn of event, there is...no justification for imposing this special levy."
Under the Sugar Protocol of the Lome Convention, Mauritius has an annual 510,000 tonnes export quota to the European Union at guaranteed prices that are higher than world market prices.
